fields.sections.2.exchanges.0.pro.words: Knechtle argues that divine image, neighbor-love, Exodus, Christ’s universal sacrifice, church equality, and Philemon jointly reveal slavery as a violation of biblical human dignity.
fields.sections.2.exchanges.0.pro.critique: Strongest feature: Knechtle builds a cumulative biblical case: God’s image establishes shared worth; neighbor-love condemns dehumanization; Exodus depicts deliverance; Christ dies for all; Galatians rejects slave-free rank in church; and Philemon receives Onesimus as a brother. Principal limitation: These themes support equal dignity without showing that every biblical regulation of slavery is morally defensible, and dismissing dissenters as unread in Philemon exceeds what the letter unambiguously proves. Live burden: Knechtle must explain how this anti-slavery canonical trajectory governs permissive legal texts and why receiving Onesimus fraternally entails rejecting the institution, not merely improving conduct within it. Locked score: The fixed 78 rewards direct moral grounding, responsiveness, and textual range while deducting for compressed inferences, unresolved contrary particulars, and overstatement about Philemon.
